To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the subgroup A‐ and subgroup B‐specific peptides 12GA and 12GB, respectively, were useful for characterization of the RSV‐specific antibody response in children with naturally occurring infection.

(i) the ELISA using peptide 12G(A), but not peptide 12G(B) was useful for the identification of children with RSV‐A infection, and (ii) the ELISA with both peptides 12G and 12G was useful for identification of children with both RSV‐A and RSV‐B infection.

the ELISA using peptide 12G(B) was a sensitive and specific test for subgroup B RSV infection in the first two epidemics, 1978–79 and 1979–80, and that the ELISA was less sensitive in subsequent epidemics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evaluation of the subgroup‐specific peptides 12G (A) and 12 G (B) as diagnostic reagents in ELISA for the characterization of the immune status of RSV‐infected children.
the development of subgroup‐specific ELISA for the G protein using synthetic peptides.

(a) the characterization of the immune responses to RSV infection in children, and (b) the evaluation of subgroup‐specific synthetic peptides of the RSV G protein for the detection of the immune response to RSV.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the ELISA using the peptide 12G(A), which is a subgroup‐A‐specific antigen, was the most sensitive method for the detection of subgroup‐A‐type RSV antibodies.
the ELISA test using the synthetic peptides 12G(B) and 12A(B) as antigens was a useful tool to characterize the immune responses of children with RSV infections.
these subgroup‐specific synthetic peptides of the RSV G protein are not suitable for the evaluation of the immune status in RSV‐infected children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
these peptides, especially peptide 12G(A), were found to be useful for the characterization of the immune responses of the RSV‐infected children.
the subgroup‐specific ELISAs with these peptides were not useful for the evaluation of the immune response of individuals to naturally occurring infection with RSV.
these peptides are not suitable as subgroup‐specific reagents for ELISA.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the subgroup‐specific peptide 12G(A), but not peptide 12G(B) or the G protein of RSV subgroup A, is an immunodominant antigen for the subgroup A virus.
the subgroup‐specific ELISA using the peptides was a sensitive and specific method for determining the immune response in children with naturally occurring respiratory syncytial viral infection.
these two peptides can be used to characterize the RSV immune response of individuals with RSV infection.
